title: Bidirectional Dijkstra in Alfama: Faster Routes! 🚦
description: Watch Bidirectional Dijkstra slice through Alfama’s winding streets by expanding search from both the start and the destination. When the two frontiers meet, the shortest path emerges with less exploration than one-way search.
ig_caption:
🚦 Bidirectional Dijkstra takes the shortest-path problem and attacks it from both ends. In Alfama’s steep, winding street graph, we run two synchronized priority queues: one forward from the start node and one backward from the goal node, each using edge weights as costs (like travel time or distance). 🧠

📍 Graph theory lens: your real map becomes a weighted graph (intersections = nodes, streets = edges). Bidirectional Dijkstra leverages optimality: when the minimum combined cost across both search frontiers is finalized at a meeting region, the algorithm reconstructs the true shortest route without exhaustively exploring the entire graph. ⚙️

If you’ve ever wondered why “meet-in-the-middle” can be dramatically faster on large graphs, this is the cleanest way to see it—step by step, frame by frame. 👀

In Lisbon’s Alfama, pathfinding becomes a real weighted graph problem: intersections are nodes, streets are edges with travel costs. Bidirectional Dijkstra improves efficiency by searching from both start and goal at once—then stitching the path together when the two frontiers meet—showing how graph search can be both optimal and fast. 💡

yt_description:
Bidirectional Dijkstra visualization in Lisbon (Alfama)! 🌍🚦

In this video, we convert real street maps into a weighted graph and run Bidirectional Dijkstra (two frontier searches from start + destination). Watch how the priority queues expand, how the meeting point determines the optimal route, and why this “meet-in-the-middle” approach reduces unnecessary exploration.
